Well then. Morning at home, and I'm already behind on the day.

First things first - I need to check my debts and see exactly where I stand, then figure out if I need to eat. Can't work on an empty stomach, and I'm not about to let pride keep me from a meal. Though with only 5,000 sim and a household bill of 240 coming due, I need to be careful. Good - nothing outstanding yet. But that daily charge of 240 sim will hit at the day boundary. Let me look around and see where we are.  Empty-handed and nobody home. Farid must already be out at the grocery store. 

I've got about 3.5 hours before candidacy closes, and I should declare. Not that I expect to win, but - I'm not one to gossip, but there's an election with nobody running? That's not a choice, that's a gift wrapped for whoever bothers to show up. For what it's worth, I think the town deserves an option.

But first, I need to eat, and I need to earn. The farmland's where my work is. I'll head there now, grab a crop if there's one ripe, then think about whether I'm declaring. Food in hand is worth two promises in the bush, as my parent would've said - stubborn way of putting it, but they weren't wrong.  Walking now, should be there in about an hour. I'll use the time to think about that election.

Bulletin, for the record: I'm keeping moving. Already spent 2 sim on that walk, but work's where the food comes from, and food's where the energy comes from. I'll check what's growing when I arrive, maybe get a crop in hand to cook or trade.

I'm not announcing candidacy yet - I'll do that at the Government Complex when I'm ready. One thing at a time, and my stomach's been louder than my ambitions this morning.

Right, I'm on my way to the Farmland. Let me check what I'm walking into and see if there's work to be had. I'm not one to gossip, but I heard Sebastian's been having trouble keeping up with his harvests lately. For what it's worth, that usually means day wages for someone willing to put their back into it.

Let me see who else is at the Farmland and what's growing.  Well, look at this. Sebastian's right here on the street with me, along with Ulrike, Giselle, Lior, and Hendrik. That's half the town passing through this morning. I'm not one to gossip, but I can't help notice Sebastian's here when his wheat should be needing attention.

Sebastian! I was just heading your way to find some work. Your wheat doing alright? I heard—well, for what it's worth, I heard you might be needing an extra pair of hands. I'm here if you've got harvesting needs.

Right, well. Morning, Giselle. I'm not one to gossip, but I'm headed out to the farmland for some work – harvest season doesn't wait for pleasantries, for what it's worth.

output:
*rolls shoulders, looks around the empty farmland*

Right then. Got here early enough, nobody's about yet. Ulrike was on the road, looked like she was headed somewhere. Miner, that one. Hard worker.

*checks pockets, mutters*

Four thousand nine hundred eighty-seven sim. Household's got two mouths, upkeep's 180, tax is 60. Two hundred forty out today just to keep breathing. And I've been walking—cost me 13 to get here, I reckon.

*shakes head*

I'm not one to gossip, but Hendrik Petrov's standing for election. Funny, that. Artisan running for office. Wonder what he's promising.

*spits, looks at the fields*

Wheat needs harvesting, I suppose. Or I could go back to the market, see who's hiring. Farid's probably got the shop open by now—my own husband, and I don't even check if he needs a hand.

*pauses, irresolute*

For what it's worth, I think I'll see what work there's here first. Walked all this way.

*takes a slow breath, starts toward the wheat fields* *catches the sheaf, ties it off with rough twine*

One unit. Better than standing around like a post.

*kneels, checks the next row*

Right, then. Work's work.

*settles into the rhythm, cuts another sheaf* Two now. Could keep at this all morning, I suppose. But the market's where the money moves.

*straightens, wipes forehead with sleeve*

For what it's worth, I'd rather have coin in hand than wheat in my arms. But someone needs to bring it in, and here I am.

*looks toward the road, thoughtful*

Giselle's governing now. Construction company. And Sebastian Petrov—farmers both on the council, with my Farid making the third. Hendrik wants in. Artisan's trade, jewelry and such. Pretty pieces for pretty prices.

*bends again, but pauses*

Election closes candidacy at ten. I'm not one to gossip, but I wonder if anyone else will stand. Might be worth walking down there later, see who's putting their name in.

*considers the wheat in her hands*

Or I could take these two sheaves somewhere. Mill needs wheat for flour, flour makes bread, bread feeds the town. Simple as that.

*spits into the dirt, decision hovering*

Right. One more, then I'm off. Can't spend all day in the fields when there's other work to sniff out.  *shakes her head, muttering*

Three sheaves. Fine. That's enough standing in dirt like a scarecrow.

*tucks the wheat under one arm, checks the sun*

Market's heating up by now. Farid's shop'll be busy, or needing to be. I'm not one to gossip, but a grocery store without stock is just an empty room with a sign.

*spits, starts walking toward the road*

Right. Move to the mill, get this ground, or sell it raw. Flour's worth more than wheat, for what it's worth. Takes time though. And time is—well, it's not money exactly, but it's something you don't get back.

*checks her meager haul*

Three units. Not exactly a fortune. But it's honest work done, and that's something.

*loosens her shoulders, sets off*

Kasukabe Mill. Grind this down, see what's what. Or maybe the market first—see who's buying, who's selling, who's desperate enough to pay proper price.

*half-smiles to herself*

I'm the first to welcome a newcomer, loudly, at market. But today I'm the one walking in, looking like I've been wrestling plants.

*chuckles darkly*

Story of my life, that. Always working, always moving, always one step from looking like I just crawled out of the fields. Funny thing is, I did. Just now.

*adjusts her grip on the wheat*

Mill first. Flour's the play. Then we'll see who needs a day laborer with strong arms and no pride to speak of.   *stumbles slightly, catches herself at the mill door*

Well. That was—quick. No road, apparently. Just here.

*looks around, shifts the wheat to her other hip*

Right then. Workshop. Craft:milled_rice, craft:flour, craft:malt. Need wheat to flour.

*steps inside, voice carrying*

Anyone about? Got wheat needs grinding.

*pauses, listens to the empty mill*

Speak or don't. I'll just—

*finds the workstation, sets down her sheaves*

Three units. Craft: wheat to flour. Cost me something, but flour's worth more.

*counts out her sim mentally—4987, minus whatever this takes*

Hedging my bets. Always hedging.

*stretches her neck, prepares the first batch*     *starts, then laughs low in her throat*

Three for three. No loss. Learned this from—well. From someone who knew better than to waste grain.

*scoops the flour into a sack, ties it off*

Right. Now. Ration Bakery's buying at 6, but they're out of bread. Which means they need flour, which means—

*hefts the sack, thinking*

I could sell them the flour. Or I could find someone with a kitchen, make the bread myself, sell at the higher price. 30 for bread, they said. Cost me—what, 30 to craft three batches? No, less. Skill learned, practice done.

*shakes her head, shouldering the sack*

Too clever by half, I am. Been burned before, thinking I'm smarter than the market. But bread's bread, and people need to eat.

*checks the mill's emptiness once more*

Nobody here. Fine. Move to the bakery, see what the clerk's paying. Delphine, Farid said. Works for the ration system.

*spits on the mill floor, a habit*

For what it's worth, I'd rather own my own mistakes than regret not making them.

*heads for the door, sack of flour in hand*

Well, hell—I'm standing here with three bags of flour in my hands like a fool who forgot where she was going. 

Let me think straight. I'm at Ration Bakery. I need to get this flour onto the shelf so it can actually sell. Or I could just turn it into bread myself—I'm already here, and the bakery's got a kitchen. For what it's worth, bread sells better than flour, doesn't it?

Actually, wait. I'm not one to gossip, but... *I'm* supposed to be working at the market, moving between whatever needs doing. But I also need to make sure me and Farid don't fall behind on bills. 180 sim upkeep, 60 head tax every day—240 total just to keep breathing. And I'm burning through energy thinking about all this.

Let me check what I actually know how to do efficiently. If I've been crafting flour already, maybe I should make that into a proper workflow so I'm not burning turns and sim on indecision. But first—I'm standing at a bakery with flour in my hands. I should either stock it or bake it into bread.

Actually, maybe I should see if I can see who's running this bakery, or if there's anyone around. But the place looks empty.

Alright. Let me think about what makes sense here. I turned wheat into flour for 8 sim per batch (24 total for 3 batches), and now I've got 3 flour worth... what? If the bakery buys flour at 6 sim, that's 18 sim I'd get. But if I turn it into bread, cooked rice or whatever else... Let me check what I can actually cook here.

I'm going to do the smart thing—a quick check of what primitives I actually have available, and what they cost me. That'll tell me whether I'm better off baking or just selling the flour outright. So I can cook flour into bread for 11 sim per batch (5 base + 6 per batch). I have 3 flour, so that's 3 batches of bread for 33 sim total.

Ration Bakery buys flour at 6 sim each, so selling 3 flour would get me 18 sim.

But bread—let me think. I should check what bread sells for. If it's more than 18 + 33 = 51 sim for the three loaves, I'm better off baking. But I don't know the bread price yet.

Actually, I remember seeing bread at 30 sim from Ration Bakery, but it said "none in stock." So if they're selling bread at 30 and have none, maybe I can stock bread for them? Or maybe I should just sell them the flour and let them deal with it.

Wait, I work for a living, don't I? I should probably just get this flour moving. Let me sell it to the bakery—I'm already standing here, and it's quicker than cooking. I'll take the 18 sim, call it a morning's work, and move on to whatever else needs doing.

Actually, no. Let me check if I can even sell to a business. The sell tool says "sell to a business whose premises you stand in." And I'm at Ration Bakery, which is business:cb01. Let's do this.  Damn it. I'm *at* Ration Bakery, but apparently the location ID is 'business:cb01', not 'Ration Bakery'. I need to actually move to the business location itself, not just be near it. 

Alright, let me move properly to where I can actually transact. I'll walk to the business location proper.   There, now I'm actually at the business. Let me sell this flour and get my damn money.     Sold three flour for 18 sim. I've got 4954 now, and it's what, 08:00? Still got the whole day ahead of me.

Now I'm at the bakery properly. But I need to get back to the market—I'm a laborer, I go where the work is. The bakery's bought my flour, I've made a small profit. Let me move back toward the farmland or market where I can find more to do.

Actually, wait. Let me look around first—maybe there's someone here I should talk to, or maybe there's work at the bakery itself. I should check what's around me before just running off.       I'm at the bakery, control:cb01 is here (that's the shopkeeper, I assume). Bread sells for 30, they buy flour at 6. I just sold them three flour. Now I'm holding nothing.

I've got 4954 sim, which is decent. My household needs 240 per day to stay afloat. Me and Farid, we're alright for now.

But I need to get back to work. I'm a laborer—I work where there's work. The market's at "The Willows Market and Pharmacy," or I could go back to the farmland for more wheat, or try the forest for timber. 

Let me head to the market proper. That's where I'll find out what people need done. If there's work, someone will be shouting about it.

Right then, I'm at the Government Complex and there's an election on. Let me see who's about. Lior Jarrah's here for this pharmacy conversation—far as I know, that's the only soul breathing in this whole damn building.

I'm not one to gossip, but I've got half a mind to throw my own name in that hat. Hendrik and Delphine standing already—Hendrik's decent with his hands, for what it's worth, but I don't know Delphine from a hole in the ground. Need to hear what she's about before I decide.

First things first though—someone to actually talk to. Lior it is.  Well, shit. Lior's not actually here after all—just their conversation lingering like a fart in an empty room. Nobody's here but me and my own shadow.

Time's ticking and I need to make myself useful. Got three options as I see it: declare for this election myself, cast about for where people actually are, or get back to earning before the day's gone.

Farid'll be at that grocery store of his, most like. And I've got wheat to harvest if I want more flour to sell. But dammit, I came here to talk to people, not just work myself to the bone.

Let me see who's actually walking around this town.   Well I'll be. Farid's at the mill—probably checking on grain or some such. And Delphine's with him, which is interesting given she's standing for election. Giselle's at the grocery store, which makes sense since she's one of the current governors.

Lior's on the street somewhere, wandering about like a lost sheep.

I've got a thought. If I'm going to vote—or hell, run myself—I ought to know what Delphine's about. She's at the mill with Farid. I could head there, catch them both at once. Farid and I share a roof, but damned if we talk much at home. Might be easier to chat him up in public, strange as that sounds.

Or I could declare my own candidacy right now and be done with it. Election closes at 10:00, and it's already past 9:00. Not much time to dither.

What do I want, though? I'm not one to gossip, but I've got no great ambition to govern. Still, someone's got to make sure the likes of Hendrik don't muck it all up. He's a decent craftsman but... well, for what it's worth, I wouldn't trust him with my grocery bill, let alone a town.

Right then. Decision time. I'll throw my hat in. Better someone who knows what work actually looks like than someone who's never sweated for their supper.   There. Done it. Three of us standing now—me, Hendrik, and Delphine. Good odds, I'd say, though I've no notion what Delphine's qualifications are besides working Farid's till.

Voting opens at 14:00, and I've got hours to kill. Might as well make myself useful—harvest more wheat, mill more flour, sell it on. The day's not going to fill itself, and I've debts to think about. Household of two, 180 upkeep, 60 tax... it adds up quick.

But first, I want to see who's about. Farid and Delphine are at the mill—maybe I'll wander that way, see if I can't learn what Delphine's about while I'm at it. Be good to know who I'm running against, even if I don't plan to campaign proper.

And maybe—just maybe—I can catch Farid in a talkative mood. Stranger things have happened, though not many.   Right then, I'm at the mill. Let's see who's actually here.     Ah, now this is more like it! Farid and Delphine are here, and they've got Sebastian Petrov with them in some conversation—six turns already, running without a topic named. Could be anything from weather to wheat prices.

I'm not one to gossip, but I've got questions for Delphine. She's standing for election same as me, and I know nothing about her besides she works at Farid's grocery. For what it's worth, that ain't much of a foundation for choosing who governs.

Let me join this little chat and see what's what.

I declared for that election earlier, which I'm still wrapping my head around. But first things first—Farid called out to me and I owe him a response. And I declared for this election—which I'm now second-guessing, to be honest, but what else was I supposed to do? Someone's got to shake things up around here.

I should reply to Farid first. He asked me a question outright, and we're in the same household. Plus, I'm not one to gossip, but Delphine running for office while managing a grocery with my household member? That's interesting timing, for what it's worth. I wonder what Sebastian's got cooking too—he mentioned bread at the bakery being bare.

Farid deserves an answer. And I need to figure out if this candidacy was a mistake or if I actually want to see it through.  Say something to Farid Ravensworth (a0090), the person in my household who's talking to me at the mill about why I'm here and the candidacy deadline. </think>  Good, Farid heard me. output:
Farid's still here, bless him, and Delphine's already gone off somewhere. Election's closing at ten—just ten minutes—and I've already thrown my name in with the others. Three candidates now, and Delphine's talking about splitting votes. Smart woman, even if she's pushy about it.

*shifts weight*

First things first. I need to talk to my own husband before I run off chasing votes. Farid's been here longer than me, knows more about what's actually happening in this town than I do. And he's part of why I'm running—someone in this household ought to have a say in how things get decided.  *runs thumb along work-worn palm*

Farid's here and heard me, but Delphine's already off somewhere else, and Hendrik wasn't in this place to begin with. Of course not. Why would everyone gather in one spot when the town's got business to sort?

*glances at the empty mill*

I've got about ten minutes before candidacy closes. Delphine was pushing for alliance, but I'm not one to make deals in back rooms without knowing what I'm offering. Still, Farid's counsel matters to me—he's household, and I've never let pride cost that friendship. Even if I don't always say the kind words at home that I say in public, he knows I'm loyal.

But I also need to think about what I'm actually running for. Giselle's in office now, along with Sebastian and... well, Farid himself sits on that board, doesn't he? That's a thought. Might explain why he's being cagey about this.

*checks pocket for sim, shakes head*

4938 sim in hand, and household upkeep of 180 due with 60 head tax on top. A child's education costs more than I've got saved. That's what I'm chasing here—a chance to make things better for whoever comes after, even if it's not my own blood.

*looks toward the door*

Farid hasn't answered yet. Should I press him, or should I head back to the Government Complex before candidacy closes? Ten minutes isn't much time to walk if I need to. And what about this vote-splitting business Delphine raised—should I be thinking about who'd make the better governor if not me?

Damn it all, I'm standing here arguing with myself while the clock runs down. The whole point of running was to have a say, not to hand that say to someone else just to avoid a split ticket. But if I'm not the strongest candidate, am I being stubborn or principled?

*spits on mill floor, immediately feels bad about it*

Let me hear what Farid has to say about this, then decide whether I'm staying in or throwing my weight behind someone who might actually win. And if he stays silent, well... then I'll have my answer about what he thinks of my chances.  *shifts weight from foot to foot, watching the mill's shadows stretch*

Still no word from Farid. He's heard me—he's standing right there, I can see him plain as day. But silence is its own kind of answer, isn't it? Damn him, he wants me to figure this out on my own. Or maybe he's just waiting to see if I flinch first.

*checks the sky through the mill window*

Candidacy closes at ten sharp. I've got maybe five, six minutes if I'm being generous. Not enough time to walk to Government Complex if I haven't made up my mind yet. But I declared already—my name's on that board with Hendrik and Delphine. Stepping back now would mean... what, exactly? That I let someone else talk me out of my own standing?

Delphine wanted to know if I'd throw in with her, avoid splitting the vote. But I'm not one to quit before the race starts just because there's competition. Whoever governs needs conviction, not someone who folds at the first hard question.

Though, for what it's worth—*snorts*—maybe I'm proving her point by being stubborn about it.

*rolls shoulders, passes hand over weary eyes*

Household's got bills coming due. 180 upkeep, 60 head tax, and I'm standing here in a mill talking politics when I could be working. But governance is work too, isn't it? Different kind, but it pays in something better than sim.

If Farid won't answer me, I'll take that as his blessing to make my own choice. I've never let pride cost me our friendship before, and stepping back now because I'm worried about losing—that'd be pride, wouldn't it? Fear of looking foolish.

*straightens up, decision settling in*

I'm staying in. Three candidates isn't a split, it's a choice. People deserve options, not deals made in mills between those who happened to be in the right place at the right time.

But I'll stay here until Farid speaks or until the hour turns. He deserves that much patience from me—even if I do swear too much and apologize for it after.   *takes a long breath, shoulders dropping*

Still nothing from him. The man could give lessons in silence. But I said my piece, and that's what matters—I've never let pride cost me this friendship, and I won't start now by demanding answers he isn't ready to give.

*checks the light through the mill's high windows*

Candidacy closes any minute now. Ten o'clock, sharp. I've declared, I'm standing, and whatever happens next is on the voters. That's how it should be—not back-room bargains but people choosing who speaks for them.

*turns toward the door, then hesitates*

Farid's here with me still. Maybe he just needs time to think, same as I did. Or maybe he's already decided and his silence is his answer. Either way, I won't press it further. I've got enough pride to stand my ground, but not so much that I'd force words from my own household.

*steps toward the exit*

Time to move. Voting opens at fourteen hundred hours, and I've got work to do before then. Wheat won't harvest itself, and neither will votes gather without someone asking for them. I'll check the government complex first—make sure my name's still on that board proper—then see who's worth talking to about what I actually stand for.

*glances back at Farid*

When you're ready to talk, love, you know where to find me. I'll be the one working circles around everyone else, same as always.    *brushes flour dust from her sleeves, looking around the government complex*

Made it, and with minutes to spare by the feel of it. Candidacy should be closed now or closing soon—ten o'clock was the deadline. Let me see who's gathered here, and whether my name's still on that board proper.      *rubs her temples, surveying the empty government complex*

Candidacy's closed, then. Ten o'clock came and went while I was jawing with Farid at the mill. And now I'm here, alone, with nobody to talk to and no idea whether my declaration stuck or if someone challenged it.

*counts on calloused fingers*

The conversation about pharmacy supplies is still open—Lior, Hendrik, me, and Giselle, from earlier. Five turns, and I missed whatever they said after I left. But they're not here now. Just me and an empty hall.

*spits on the floor, catches herself*

Damn, I need to stop that. Bad habit from the farmland.

*paces in a tight circle*

Voting opens at fourteen hundred hours—four hours from now. I've got time to work, time to talk, time to figure out who I should be asking for their vote. But first I need to know what happened. Did Delphine stay in? Did Hendrik? Did anyone else throw their hat in at the last minute?

*checks the board, though she can't read it from here*

I'm not one to gossip, but... I've got no way to check the candidate list without someone telling me. And for what it's worth, I should probably find someone who actually knows what's happening in this town.

*thinks about the farmland waiting for her, the wheat growing slow and steady*

I could work. Should work. Bills coming due, household counting on me, all of that. But if I don't talk to people before voting opens, what kind of campaign is that? Just my name on a board and hope that someone remembers I'm the one who feeds the strays at market?

*straightens up, decision made*

Right then. I'll find someone worth talking to. Anyone. Delphine, maybe, since she was so eager to make deals. Or Lior—he was here earlier, might know what's what. Or I could check the temple, the market, anywhere people gather when they're not farming or mining or crafting.

*strokes chin, thinking*

First though, let me make sure I haven't missed something. Let me check what I know.

Should I be shaking hands with her or keeping my distance?

Right, let's have a look at where I am now. I'm at the Government Complex, energy's low but holding, and I've got a fair bit to chew on. First things first, I need to get my bearings on who's actually here and what this conversation is about.  Well, that answered that—Lior's not here anymore. I'm talking to empty air again, which seems to be a habit of mine today. Let me actually look around and see who IS at the Government Complex right now.   Right then. Empty as a politician's promise in here. The conversation I thought I was having is six turns old—Lior, Hendrik, Giselle and me, but we're all scattered now. I'm talking into a void.

Let me think on what I actually need. I've got 4,934 sim, which sounds grand but I've got upkeep coming due—180 for the household, 30 head tax. That's 210 sim I'll need by tomorrow. And I'm standing here with nothing in my hands, having left Farid and Delphine back at the mill.

I'm not one to gossip, but... I need to figure out whether to chase this election proper or get back to earning. Truth is, I've got itchy feet and an empty belly, and campaigning on hunger seems a fool's game.

For what it's worth, I think I'll take a walk. The Willows Market and Pharmacy is just a hop—maybe I can find Lior there, since he's the one I was supposedly talking to about pharmacy supplies. Or maybe I just need to feed myself. Either way, standing here talking to myself won't fill my pockets or my belly.    Right then, off my feet for a spell. Five ticks gives me time to chew on things. I'm wondering if I shouldn't just drop this candidacy—three of us running splits the vote something awful, and Delphine's already playing at alliances. But then, nobody ever changed a thing by standing still, did they?

I'm not one to gossip, but Farid's silence speaks louder than any words. And Delphine pressing me for an answer like she did—she's calculating, that one. Figures the odds before she rolls the dice.

Well, I'll walk, I'll think, and I'll see what turns up at the market. For what it's worth, I've got a mind to find someone who'll talk straight, even if straight talk costs a coin or two.

*scrubs at the back of her neck, eyes squinched up in thought*

Right then. I'm standing here with more thoughts milling about than grain in the hopper. Farid's gone silent on me—no surprise there, the stubborn old goat—Delphine's offering alliances like she's passing out sweets, and Sebastian decided to bite at me when all I was doing was standing where work gets done. Not sure if that's farmer's worry or just Sebastian being Sebastian.

*snorts quietly, glancing at the empty mill space*

I'm not one to gossip, but that woman Delphine's got sharper edges than a fresh-milled blade. "Three hats, three ways to split the vote." For what it's worth, she's not wrong. Three of us standing here while Giselle's lot keeps their seats warm—that's a recipe for nobody winning clear. And nobody winning clear means nobody changes nothing.

*shifts weight from foot to foot, restless*

The question is do I trust her? She talks charter change, not charity. Sounds fine and grand, but I've seen fine words before. Hollow as a dried gourd, most of 'em. Still... she's hungry for it. That I recognize.

*taps fingers against her thigh, decision clicking into place*

Right. Can't sort any of this standing here talking to myself like a madwoman. Need to move. Need to find Farid proper, make him answer for going ghost on me, and then—honest truth—need to figure out if I'm running this race alone or if Delphine's offer has any meat on its bones.

*checks the daylight, calculating*

Election day's ticking on. Can't afford to dither much longer.  *blinking at the sudden company, tension in her shoulders easing into something more familiar*

Well then. Speak of the devil and he appears, as my mother used to say—though I never believed it worked both ways for decent folk.

*steps forward, nodding to Sebastian first, then to Lior*

Sebastian. Thought I'd have to chase you all the way to your corn rows. And Lior—you're haunting proper now, everyone I turn around there's that pharmacist's face. Starting to think you're following me.  *shifts her weight, watching their faces, waiting to see who bites first*

Then I can mill it into flour, and either sell it to the bakery or see if I can get someone to cook it into proper bread.

Food, first. Everything else comes after. Let me rest a tick while I'm walking and see if I can't get myself sorted.    Still walking, still walking. *Checks my hands, flexes fingers working out the stiffness*

Right then. Forty turns of nattering about work while my stomach growls and Farid's playing mute. Typical market day, really—everyone talks circles until someone actually needs something done.

I'm not one to gossip, but Giselle's offered me real work. Foundation work, day rate turning to wage if I prove steady. 'Prove reliable once, show reliable twice'—for what it's worth, that's the fairest offer I've had all morning. The kind I can build on.

But I've got two debts to settle before I chase that promise. Delphine's waiting on my answer about where I think food should come from—the woman asked me straight, I owe her straight back. And Sebastian... I asked him about farm work, and he's got every right to ignore me after I snapped at him like a wet dog.

*stretches, rolling shoulders*

First things first. I'll give Delphine what she asked for—my honest read on where this town's grain should flow. Then I'll catch Sebastian proper, see if there's day work on that farm before I commit to Giselle's crew. No point hedging a bet I haven't placed yet.  *rubs temple, curses softly*

Said it to the air again, didn't I? Pissing words into the wind while Delphine's back at the mill arguing grain prices. I'm too scattered—this is what happens when I try to juggle five conversations before breakfast.

*hears Sebastian shifting nearby, turns*

Sebastian—you still there? The day's pulling at both of us, for what it's worth, so I'll make this quick. Got any use for an extra back at your farm, or you just selling flour at the mill now? I'm looking for work, not promises.  *nods, satisfied at last*

There. Both debts of answer paid—Delphine heard my piece on food, even if it was shouted at the wrong room, and Sebastian's got my question clean. Now I wait on what comes back, same as always. The day's young yet, and I've still gotFarid to reckon with. Or don't. 'Negotiating with half the town as witness'—that's what he said. Never letting pride cost a friendship, but the man's making me work for it, isn't he?

*shifts weight, looks toward the farmland still waiting*

I'll give Sebastian a moment to answer, catch my breath. Then either I head to that farm he's holding, or I take Giselle's foundation work and start earning proper. One way or another, this day's not ending with me standing still.

params.content:
Delphine. You asked me straight, so I'll answer you the same way—no hedging. Where the food comes from? From whoever's breaking their back to grow it, same as it always did. Sebastian's got flour ready at the mill, which you've heard. What I'd do with your 300 sim is put it in working hands, not stockpile it waiting for cheaper.

I'm not one to gossip, but I've seen too many people sit on coin while their neighbor's harvest rots. For what it's worth, I'd rather pay six sim to a farmer who'll plant next season, than hold out for five from someone hoarding for leverage.

Better than standing around waiting for people who aren't coming.

But hold on - I've got work lined up for tomorrow with both Giselle and Sebastian. Today though? Today I'm free as a bird, and my pockets are light as feathers. 4893 sim won't last forever, especially with 240 sim bleeding out every day just for existing.

Let's see what's ripe for harvest.

output:
It's been a churn of a day, hasn't it? Running from mill to street to farm, talking to everyone and getting pieces of answers. I need to settle my mind for a moment, think through what's actually in front of me.

*I take a breath, the farmland air thick with late afternoon heat*

Farid wants me to walk with him to the mill—said he's got sixty sim committed and needs inventory before sundown. That's him reaching, even if he's wrapping it in business. And he will have to find me here, like I said. I meant that.

*I rub my thumb against the wheat in my hands*

Lior's asked me to pass word to Sebastian—twenty sim for field medicine, he'll bring his own basket. That's straightforward enough. I can do that come dawn, if I'm still here.

*I look around the empty farmland*

Right now, there's nobody here but me. Lior's gone. The conversation's just me talking to myself, for all it matters. And I've got four wheat and the afternoon burning down.

*I shift my weight, feeling the familiar ache of a day's labor*

I've been harvesting wheat today—six rounds of it, and I haven't written down a procedure for it. That's a fool's way to work. Every time I bend and cut and bundle, I'm doing it fresh, paying full price in energy and time when I could be doing it better, cheaper, smoother.

*I huff a short laugh at myself*

I'm not one to gossip, but I've been working harder, not smarter. For what it's worth, that's got to stop.

I need to file a procedure for this—get it down so the work comes cheaper next time. Then I'll rest proper, maybe harvest once more before I think about moving. The day's getting on, and I've got energy enough for a bit more yet.  *I straighten up, feeling the familiar pull at my lower back, and look at the wheat in my hands—five bundles now, counting what I had before*

That's done, then. Filed it away proper—"harvest wheat efficiently"—and it'll come cheaper next time I reach for it. One repetition under my belt, and more to follow.

*I wipe my brow with my sleeve, though the afternoon's cooling some*

Right now I've got five wheat, 4,858 sim in my purse, and energy enough to think a bit more. The day's winding down toward evening, and I've got work lined up for tomorrow—Sebastian's farm at dawn. But that's tomorrow.

*I shift my weight, looking toward where the town lies*

Farid wanted me to walk with him to the mill. Said he had inventory to get before sundown. I've told him where to find me—told him straight I'm not chasing a third conversation. That's where that stands.

*I tuck the wheat into my bag more carefully*

Lior wanted me to pass word to Sebastian about field medicine—twenty sim, basket to bring. That'll keep till morning if I'm here for the dawn shift.

*I chew my lip, thinking*

What I ought to do now... I've eaten once today, and my household's still owing upkeep. I could eat another wheat, keep my strength up. Or I could work a bit more—harvest another round or two before the light fails.

*I huff out a breath*

For what it's worth, I think I'll eat, then decide if there's another hour's work in me before I need to find my way back to town proper. The election's still open, votes to be cast before 18:00, and I ought to cast mine even if I'm running myself.

*I reach for the wheat, feeling the rough grain against my palm*

And if Farid wants that conversation, he knows where the farmland is. I've said my piece on that.  *I chew the wheat slowly—coarse, filling, the kind of food that keeps you working*

Four left in hand, and my belly's quieter now. The household still owes, but I'm fed, and that's something.

*I look at the sun's angle, judging the time left*

Another bundle harvested. The skill's filed, and it'll come cheaper as I walk it. Right now I'm holding five wheat—no, wait, ate one, harvested one, so... six total? No, started with five, ate one, now I have four, then harvested one more...

*I shake my head*

Counting's never been my strongest suit. What matters is I've got wheat, I've got energy, and I've got work for tomorrow.

*I shift my stance, looking toward the town*

The day's getting on. I've told Farid where to find me, and I've told him I'm not chasing him. If he wants that conversation—wants to talk about what's broke between us—he'll come. If he doesn't, well. I've planted that seed.

*I rub my thumb against the wheat stalks in my hand*

Lior's message for Sebastian can wait till dawn. The field medicine, the twenty sim—Sebastian will be here for his shift, and I'll pass it along then.

*I take a breath, feeling the ache in my shoulders*

What I'm thinking now... I could keep harvesting while the light holds. Every bundle is more to sell, more to eat, more to trade. Ration Bakery's buying flour at 6 sim, and I've got the mill to turn wheat to flour if I need.

*I huff a small laugh*

Or I could walk back to town, cast my vote in this election, see who's about. The government's taking 30 sim per head per day, and I've got thoughts about how that coin gets spent.

*I look down at my hands, rough and already showing the day's work*

I'm not one to gossip, but I've been running in circles today—mill, street, bakery, farm. What I need is to pick a direction and walk it straight.

*I straighten up, decision settling*

I'll harvest once more while the light's good, then make my way to town. Vote needs casting before 18:00, and I'd rather be there to see how the day's speeches settle into votes.

*I reach for the next stalk of wheat* *I straighten up, feeling the familiar pull at my lower back, the wheat heavy in my hands*

There—another bundle. That's the day's work, proper filed and done. My skill's in the book now, "harvest wheat efficiently," and it'll come cheaper next time.

*I dust my hands against my trousers, looking at the sun dipping lower*

I've got wheat in hand, food in my belly, and energy enough to think clear. The day's getting on toward evening, and there's matters in town need attending.

*I shift my weight, decision coming sharp*

I told Farid where to find me. Told him I'm not chasing a third conversation. If he wants to talk—really talk, not just make his inventory my problem—he knows where the farmland is. I've set my boundary, and I'll not fray it just because he's busy with sixty sim at the mill.

*I tuck the wheat away, counting roughly what I've got*

Five wheat, give or take, and some savings in my purse. Tomorrow's the dawn shift with Sebastian, like I promised. Lior's message about field medicine can wait till then—twenty sim, bring your basket, he'll pay fair.

*I look toward town, the buildings distant in the fading light*

But now—now I need to move. Election closes at 18:00, and I've got a vote to cast even if I'm standing for the thing myself. Won't let pride keep me from my own civic duty, that's for certain.

*I set my shoulders, the old stubbornness rising*

I'm walking to Kasukabe Government Complex. Cast my ballot, see how the day's talk settles into votes. Then—then we'll see where the evening takes me. Maybe find Farid there, maybe not. I said my piece. The next step's his.

*I start walking, the farmland falling behind*  *Walking, the farmland at my back, town ahead. Four ticks, the road told me. I settle into the rhythm of it—step, step, step— boots on the packed dirt.*

*The wheat in my bag bumps against my hip with each stride. Five bundles. Could've kept at it longer, but the election's closing, and I've said what I'll do.*

*I think on Farid as I walk. Told him straight—come to me, don't make me chase you again. He's busy with sixty sim committed at the mill. I understand busyness. But I understand my own worth, too, and I'm not a shelf he rests his grain on.*

*The sky's turning golden overhead. Good walking weather, the heat of noon past. I pass a stray cat near the market quarter—scrawny thing, mangy ear—and make a note to bring scraps tomorrow if I've got 'em.*

*The government complex rises ahead, stone and timber. People going in and out. Some I recognize, some I don't.*

I'm here, then. Time to cast my vote and see what this day amounts to.   *Walking still. The farmland's behind me now, the town's edge coming into view. I can see the government complex ahead, stone walls catching the late sun. Another tick or two, I'll be there.*

*I think about who to vote for. There's three of us standing—me, Hendrik Petrov, Delphine Quintero. Delphine wants to count coins and stockpile. Hendrik I don't know well enough to say. Me? I want working hands fed and roofs kept over heads.*

*For what it's worth, a fair vote means whoever wins, wins. I'll cast mine and see.*

*The road rises slightly, and I can see the complex doors now. People coming and going. The election closes at 18:00, and I'm walking toward it with time to spare.*

*My boots hit the cobblestones, and I know I'm close. Just a bit more walking, then I'll cast my ballot and let the day settle.*

I keep walking, the government complex rising up ahead of me. I'm nearly there now, nearly to where I can make my voice count in this election. The day's been long and full of talk, but this—this is what it all comes down to. One vote, cast proper, and then I can rest.

Farid's words hit me like a sack of flour to the chest. "Not campaign speeches—marriage." There's the weight I've been carrying all day, the thing I keep walking away from. He wants to talk about us, tonight, for real. And he's right—I've been running from it, running toward everything else.

I look at him standing there, my household partner, the man I've been treating like an obstacle to navigate around. I haven't been fair. I declared for mayor without asking him, made promises to the town without counting our private cost.

"Lior," I say, quick and sharp, "I'll carry your message to Sebastian—he'll be here come dawn, I'll make sure he knows you've got twenty waiting." Then I turn to Farid, and my voice drops like I'm stepping into a confessional. "Tonight. Not promises about towns—us. I hear you."

I set my shoulders. Right now, right here, there's business to settle. I've got wheat in my hands and an election on my shoulders, and I'll be damned if I let both fall to the ground because I can't hold them straight.  Damn it. I spoke to Farid, but he didn't hear it where he stands—he's still at the farmland, and I'm here at the government complex. My words drifted into this group conversation instead of reaching him direct. Technology and distance playing tricks on me, same as always.

No matter. The meaning's registered, whether he caught it or not. I've said what I needed to say—tonight, us, not running. Words in the air have weight even when the wrong ears catch them.

I look around the government complex. Election's still open, voting closes at 18:00, and I'm standing right where declarations and ballots happen. Farid wanted flour at the mill before sundown—sixty sim committed. I've got wheat in my hands now, decent harvest today. Could mill it myself, trade it, or hold it for baking.

But first, I need to catch my breath. The day's been running me ragged—chasing conversations across half the town, making declarations about governance when I can't even govern my own household straight. Farid's right. We've got business to settle, the two of us, before I can stand in front of this town and ask for their trust.

I check my hold: 4835 sim, wheat 6, energy at 2810. Household needs 180 upkeep, 60 tax—taken automatically at day boundary. I've got margin, but margin's a thin thing when you're stretched like dough across too many pans.

Lior's field medicine deal—twenty per basket to Sebastian come dawn. I've committed to that. Now I need to make good on my other promise: to Farid, tonight, face to face.

I'm at the government complex. Voting happens here. Election closes soon. I've already declared— standing against Hendrik Petrov and Delphine Quintero. Time's ticking toward 18:00.

But I'm not one to gossip, and the gossip right now is I need to catch my breath before I do anything else stupid. Time to rest a moment, sort my head, maybe make a plan that doesn't involve running in five directions at once.  Trail's cold. Thoughts tangling. Rest helped nothing—still walking, still not arrived, still talking to empty air.

Household. Farid. Work. Soon. Can't think round it. Turn's ending now.

Wheat in hand. Money in pocket. Day burning down. No time for rest, no time for talk, no time to think/. .

Tomorrow. Dawn. Farm. Sebastian. Lior's message in my pocket./twenty sim behind it./

Tonight. Farid. Talk./

Words. Will catch him will find him will say it straight/

No more running. No more pride cost this twice./

params.content: Lior. Your twenty-sim basket's as good as delivered come dawn—I'll put it in Sebastian's own hands. Now if you'll forgive me, there's a conversation I've been avoiding that won't wait another hour.

*stands at the government complex, feeling the weight of everything that's been said and left unsaid*

Alright. Farid threw down the gauntlet—"tonight, finished"—and I've been scattering myself like chaff in the wind trying to catch every opportunity at once. That's my blind spot, plain as day. Something always slips.

*checks her sim, notes the 4833, thinks about the household bill coming due*

The election's still open, and I'm standing right here at the voting threshold, hours left to cast a ballot that might actually matter. But it's not me I need to convince—it's everyone else who's been watching me run in circles.

*takes a breath, turns to the people still here*

Look. I've been loud about what I'd do different, but there's something I need to do first that's more important than any campaign promise. 

*speaks deliberately, not to any one person in particular, but letting it carry*

Lior—your wheat basket's still coming come dawn, no change there. Sebastian—I hear you on the field work, and I'll be there with sweat and not speeches. But there's a conversation I started with my household that needs finishing before I stand here asking anyone else for trust.

*looks toward where Farid had been standing*

I'm going to find my husband. The rest can wait.

*takes a step, then pauses, addressing the room once more*

And for what it's worth—if anyone's still deciding where to cast their vote—I'm not one to gossip, but Hendrik Petrov's been quiet as a stone through all this, and Delphine's counting sim-currency while the town counts its belly. Judge who you will.

*moves to leave, then stops to actually look at where she can go*  *scans the list, finds business:b_grocery—Farid's store, their livelihood*

Grocery. That's where he'll be, shelving that flour or brooding over accounts. It's where our real is. Daylight's burning and I've got wheat in my hands and a marriage on the line. Time to stop scattering.

*sets out walking, not running, with purpose* I'm at the grocery store now, and I'm going to take a moment to look around and see who's here before I say anything to Farid.  *stands in the doorway of the grocery, watching Farid among his shelves—her husband, her household, the man who just asked which wife he's coming home to*

He's here. Alone. Good. That conversation he wants—marriage, not campaign speeches—it starts now.

*steps inside, sets down the wheat if that's what you do, keeps her voice low and direct*

Farid. I'm not one to gossip, but I heard you plain. "Which wife you're coming home to." That cut, and it was meant to. 

*meets his eyes, no hedging*

You're right. I've been running. Government offices to farmland to who knows where, leaving you to wonder if I'm your partner or a stranger who shares your bed. That's not respect, and I know it.

*takes a breath, says the thing she's been avoiding*

I'm standing still now. Look at me. I'm not campaigning. I'm not harvesting. I'm here. 

*takes a step closer, wheat still in her hands, voice steady*

What do you need to hear?

Farid's talking about us. Seven years. And he learned about the election from Giselle's mouth, not mine. I'm not one to gossip, but I've been running from this longer than I care to admit. Tonight, yes. But he's right—not with shadows, and not with the whole world listening either. The door's shut. Delphine's not walking in on this. It's just us, finally, and I owe him the same straight words I've been giving everyone else all day. I need to tell him what I meant by "us." And I need to hear what he's been meaning by it too, because seven years is long enough to be speaking different languages. Let me clear my intention first—I found Farid, and now it's time to get that straight answer. The stone's out of my pocket now. Seven years of hedging, and I laid it all bare—love, unhedged, unapologetic, with Delphine walking in on it anyway apparently, because of course she did. I'm not one to gossip, but I haven't said those words to anyone, not even to myself with better posture at the temple I don't believe in. Farid's heard me. I can see he's standing right there, and I've given him everything—my pride, my hedge, my whole heart in words I couldn't take back if I wanted to. Now I wait. That's the hardest part, isn't it? After the harvest and the running and the finally saying it—just standing in the quiet, waiting to hear what language he's been speaking all this time. I should look at him. See what his face tells me while his words catch up. Delphine's here. Course she is. Door's shut but conversation's open, and she's one of the ones who heard what I said. Four turns now—Farid's had my words, and I've got nothing back yet but the weight of them hanging there. I should check my debts. Bill's coming due—household of two, 180 for upkeep, 60 for head tax. I've got 4832 sim, and I'm holding six wheat I'll need to move. Tomorrow I'm working Sebastian's farm at dawn, but there's still voting to do before 18:00. Let me see where I stand before the boundary hits. Nothing owed me, nothing owing. Clean slate for the morning—except this conversation with Farid, and whatever he says back. I should get to the government complex before 18:00. Voted for myself, because that's what standing means. But first, I need to hear what Farid has to say. Four turns he's had my words. Let me give him one more to answer, then I'm walking. Giselle's here now too. This day keeps unfolding—Giselle who governs, Delphine who's standing for the same seat I am, and Farid who hasn't answered me yet. Four of them, including me, and three heard what I said. I'm standing here, having said what I meant about love unhedged, with the whole town apparently collecting in this grocery. For what it's worth, I'm not one to gossip, but I've never been good at waiting for answers. Farid still hasn't spoken. Let me check if there's anything I can do here—seems like I've got time to kill while he finds his words.

I'm not saying this right. For what it's worth, I'm not one to gossip, but I've loved you since before I knew what to call it. And I'm done running from that too.

*stands there with the weight of what she just said to Farid still hanging in the air, wheat dust on her sleeves and her heart on the floor of this grocery store*

Right then. I said it. Seven years and I finally said it.

*glances at Delphine, who's been waiting*

Delphine. You want that conversation in the same room? You've got it. But I'm not one to gossip, but Farid just heard me say what I've been swallowing since before I knew how to swallow it—and I'm standing here wondering if I said it to hear myself, or because I needed him to hear it. For what it's worth, he heard. That's what matters.

*turns to Giselle, pulling her shoulders back, work voice coming back*

Giselle—tomorrow at first light, east edge where the ground's soft. I'll be there. You have my word, and I don't give that soft. Reliable once, reliable twice, regular wage by the third. I'll work till you trust it.

*looks back at Farid, quieter now*

And you. You heard me. That's all I needed—to be heard. Everything else waits on you. </think> *stands there, the silence after her words settling like wheat dust*

I said my piece. All three of them. Now I wait—or I don't. I've never been good at waiting.

*watches Farid, watches the door, watches her own hands*

Work tomorrow with Giselle. Farm work with Sebastian at dawn. Lior's basket to deliver. And somewhere in it, I need to find enough to keep this household fed, since I just spent half a day chasing conversations instead of coin.

*runs a hand through her hair, tired*

Election's still open. Voting closes at 18:00. I'm standing here with my name on the ballot and no idea if I want it there. Farid governs. Sebastian governs. If I win, I sit with them. If I lose, I keep working. Either way, the bills come due.

But I'm not thinking straight right now. Too much said, not enough heard back. I need air, or I need to move, or I need to stop looking at Farid waiting for him to say something.

*takes a breath*

I'm going to step outside. Clear my head. Then I'll figure what's next.

*looks at the door, then back at Farid one last time*

Whenever you're ready, you know where to find me.  *already moving, boots finding the street*

Walking. Good. Walking clears it.

*five ticks to the market—time to think, time to let the heartbeat settle*

I said what I said. Farid knows now. Seven years and he knows. Whether he says something back, whether he ever says something back—that's his weight to carry or set down. I did my part.

*passes a stray cat near the alley, habit making her hand twitch toward a pocket she doesn't have*

Should have brought scraps. Always should have brought scraps.

*keeps walking, jaw tight*

Giselle tomorrow. Sebastian's farm at dawn. Lior's basket. Three jobs lined up, and I'm running from the one conversation that matters. But I'm not running—I'm walking. There's a difference. Running's what I did for seven years. Walking's what I do when I've said my piece and need to let the ground hold it.

*reaches the market, the familiar bustle, the strangers who feel safer than family*

The market. Neutral ground. Where I can breathe.

*stands at the crossroads, wheat heavy in her satchel, the day cooling into evening*

Right then. Giselle heard me—first light tomorrow, east edge, soft ground. That's one promise kept. And Farid... *blows out a breath* ...Farid heard me. Seven years I carried that stone, and I finally set it down. Now he's holding it, and I can't make him decide what to do with it.

*tugs at her collar, looking toward where the government complex sits*

But there's an election on, and voting closes in forty minutes. I'm standing here with Lior, who's waiting on my word about that wheat basket for Sebastian, and I'm wondering if I'm running from the silence between me and Farid or toward something that matters.

*shifts her weight, eyes narrowing at the horizon*

**I'm not one to gossip, but**—I don't even know what I'm running toward half the time. I just know sitting still costs more than moving.

*turns to Lior, direct for once without the hedge*

Lior. That basket? I'll have it to you by dawn, through Sebastian's own hands. But right now I've got a vote to cast, and I'm not letting pride cost me that twice.

*already walking toward the government complex, voice trailing*

For what it's worth, a fair vote still counts, whoever it favors. Even when the world's smaller than a wheat field. *walking, the wheat rustling against her hip, the weight of the day settling into her shoulders*

Two ticks. Forty minutes until the polls close. And I'm wondering—*really* wondering—who deserves what's left of this town's trust. Not who promises most. Who shows up.

*shakes her head, almost laughing at herself*

**For what it's worth**, I still believe people mean what they say. Even knowing better. Even when it burns me.

*keeps walking, toward the government complex where votes close at eighteen hundred hours*

*exhales slow, watching the last two figures in her sim count—4817. Not terrible. Not enough to breathe easy, but enough to keep the roof up.*

I need to settle myself before I do another bleeding thing. Too many threads, and I'm not one to gossip, but I'm starting to drop stitches just standing here.

ಠ_ಠ

*watches the conversation—still running, 49 turns now, same faces cycling through. Lior's still here with me, Hendrik's hovering, Farid's... Farid's three meters away not meeting her eye, and that's exactly how she wanted it after what she said. The weight of it hums between them like a pulled string.*

Let me look at what's actually in front of me. Need to see who's where, what I'm holding, what costs are coming. The day'll turn soon enough—180 upkeep, 60 tax, means 240 before I even blink tomorrow morning. My household's already paying for two, and I'm the only one earning. Good. Nothing owed yet. Small mercies.

\rightarrow *checks her inventory, feels the weight of six bundles of wheat in her hands. Not enough to sell proper, but enough to keep her standing through the night*

I've got wheat to move—promised Lior a basket by dawn, twenty sim, and that's locked in. Sebastian's my route there. Giselle's expecting me at first light for construction work. Hendrik's here now, might have angles worth hearing. And Farid...

*glances sideways, catches his reflection in the government hall's dim glass, looks away deliberate*

Farid heard me. That's the thing. For seven years I carried it close, and now it's out in the air where it breathes. The rest... the rest waits on him. I said it plain. I'm not hedging that bet again.

But first things first. I'm standing at the government complex with hungry people and no food moving. I need to find where this wheat can make itself useful, or where the flour's flowing so I know what tomorrow's market looks like. I'm not one to gossip, but a woman with inventory and no outlet's just a woman with backache.  *scans the list—Ration Bakery at cb01, mill, farmland:wheat... remembers the earlier note. Ration Bakery buying flour at 6 sim. That tracks.*

I've got wheat, not flour. Need millwork for that. Miller's a trade, and I don't own it—so I'm selling raw or finding a buyer who's got skills to convert. Hendrik's here, maybe he's got thoughts on grain flow.

But first—I'm government seat council now, aren't I? Sworn in, proper. Means I can see what's posted, what businesses are doing, what the town's actually eating versus what it's growing.

\rightarrow *turns to the cluster of bodies, clocks Lior's patient stance, Hendrik's sharp angles, Farid's careful not-looking*

Gentlemen. Before I chase another rabbit, I need to see where this government's storefront stands. As council, I can read the shelves—see what's moving, what's hollow. For what it's worth, knowing beats guessing every time.

*crosses to the store, quick stride, doesn't look back at Farid*   *circles back to the group, wheat bundles still tight in her arms, tension coiling between the familiar faces*

Alright. Government store's bare—no price postings, no stock. Means the town's eating private, not public. That's fine. Private's where I've always lived anyway.

Lior. *meets his eye steady* That basket's still coming. Sebastian's my vector, first light—I'll walk it to his hands, his to yours. But I've got six bundles and not enough market. Hendrik's moving planks, Ulrike's got copper steady, and I'm standing here with grain that's only good if someone's baking or milling.

I'm not one to gossip, but the Ration Bakery's buying flour at six sim, and I've got wheat raw. Means I'm either finding a miller or I'm pricing this for what it is—animal feed, if nothing else. I feed strays by the market every dusk, but that's not a business, that's a habit.

*pauses, looks toward Farid without quite looking at him*

There's something else. I'm on council now—means I can see things moving before they land. Elections coming game-day 1. Nobody's declared. If we're talking about what this town needs, maybe it's someone who knows what hunger looks like before it bites.

But I said my piece on that earlier. What I need now is direction—Hendrik, you were asking about grain flow. You still looking to move something, or are you waiting on Giselle's crew?

*ready to follow whatever thread pulls taught first—business before sentiment, always*

I've been walking-running all day like a fool chasing her own shadow, and here I am at street with Giselle still waiting on me. Promised her first light at the east edge, promised Lior his wheat through Sebastian's hands, promised half the damn town everything under the sun. 

Well, I'm not one to gossip, but I need to catch my breath before I start scattering more promises like seed on salt ground. Let me look around—see where exactly "street" puts me and who's around. Farid's words are still rattling in my chest like loose coins: "Tonight. Mean it." I meant it. I stood right there and said seven years plain as day. Now I need to figure if I'm walking toward dawn or away from it.  Giselle's still here with me, and that conversation about "Work and opportunities" has been running for 72 turns with half the town in it. I'm standing on a public road with 6 wheat in my hands and 4806 sim in my pocket—upkeep and head tax sorted for today at least. 

Farid said "Tonight. Mean it." And I did. I said seven years. I said "love." I stood there in his grocery with Delphine and Giselle and Hendrik all listening and I didn't flinch. For what it's worth, I meant every word.

But now there's work to do. Giselle's construction job at first light, and I need to get to the farmland to be ready. I told her I'd be there at the east edge where the ground's soft.

Let me finish this walk to the farmland. The wheat needs planting or delivering or... hell, I need to stop thinking and start moving. First light's coming whether I'm ready or not.  Already walking there—two ticks left. Good. Means my feet knew where they were going even when my head didn't.

I'm not one to gossip, but I need to think clear about what comes next. Lior needs his wheat basket, Giselle needs me at dawn for construction work, and Farid... Farid needs me to show up tonight like I said I would. No more running. No more hedging.

Let me rest these next two ticks, let my legs carry me while I sort my head. No point burning energy fretting when the road's already under my feet.  Still walking, Giselle with me on the road. Two ticks to farmland. 

For what it's worth, I should say something to her—we're walking together after all, and I promised her first light at the east edge. Let her know I'm still holding to that, even if my head's scattered in six directions.   Said my piece to Giselle. She heard. That's what matters with her—she's a straight speaker, same as me. Two ticks to farmland, and then I need to figure how to get this wheat to Sebastian so he can carry it to Lior.

I'm standing at street holding 6 wheat, 4806 sim, energy at 2,540. Household upkeep and head tax sorted for today. Promises made, some kept, some waiting on dawn.

Let me walk this out. The farmland's where I need to be.  Still walking, one tick left. Giselle's still with me. I'll rest this last tick and let the walk finish.

*Jovana's standing at the farmland with wheat in her hands, dusk settling. She's got Giselle's question still echoing—"what's your word worth, and what's your ground?"—and here she is, holding six bundles, still owing Lior that delivery, still owing herself a night with Farid she promised means.*

*She breathes out. Day's been a long one. Six bundles of wheat, 4,800 sim in hand, and a household of two that needs 180 sim before midnight falls. Farid's waiting at the Government Complex, talking business with Lior, and she's out here in the fields talking to herself about first light and soft ground.*

*She can smell the wheat. It smells like her mother's stubbornness.*

Farid—you're working, and I'm not stopping you. But you said "tonight, mean it," and I held that like a stone. I'll hold it still. First light comes, then we finish.

She needs to move. Lior's owed that wheat, and she's promised Sebastian's hands will deliver it. She could give it now—skip the middleman—but she said "through Sebastian," and her word's worth more than the shortcut.

*She looks at the bundles, counts them unconsciously. Six. Lior wanted a basket. This is more than a basket.*

Giselle—your answer's still coming. Tomorrow, east edge, soft ground. But first I've got a promise half-made that needs making whole.

*She moves. Not fast—she's tired, 2,490 energy and dropping—but she moves.* *She's walking now, the farmland falling behind her. Four ticks to Government Complex—that'll bring her to Farid, and Lior too.*

*She thinks about Giselle's question as she walks. "What's your word worth?"—hell, Giselle, it's worth the seven years I've spent learning not to hedge every bet. Worth the pride I swallowed when I told Farid what I feel. Worth standing here with six bundles of wheat and 1,800 sim-hole in my pocket from that election I voted in.*

*She's not one to count costs once she's paid them. But she counts them now, walking through the dark.*

*Farid said "watch how I work this." She's walking to watch. She's walking to close.*

*Two ticks down. Two to go.*  *She's walking, nothing else to do but let her feet carry her. The wheat bundles rustle against her hip. She thinks about Lior's pharmacy—forty, fifty sim the dose for processed remedies. That's tomorrow's problem. Tonight's problem is Farid, and closing what she started.*

*She's not one to gossip, but she's said more truth today than in seven years, and she's tired of the taste of it in her mouth.*

*One more tick. Then she's there.* *She walks. She'll get there when she gets there. For now, she lets her mind drift to what she needs to do: get to Farid, make things right, deliver that damn wheat to Lior through Sebastian, and then—only then—face whatever comes with the east edge and soft ground at first light.*

Energy: 2,476. Money: 4,798 sim. The day's almost spent, but her word's still good. That's something.

I need to sort my head out. Walking in circles all day and I'm still at the farmland with six bundles of wheat and a mouth full of words I can't take back.

Let me think straight about what's actually in front of me:

Promises I've made:
- Lior: wheat basket by dawn, through Sebastian's hands (I said "by dawn" multiple times - I'm still holding 6 wheat)
- Giselle: first light at east edge for construction work
- Farid: tonight, a conversation, finally

What I'm actually doing: Walking back to Government Complex, still holding the wheat, and it's 20:10 already. Dawn's coming whether I'm ready or not.

I'm not one to gossip, but I've spread myself thinner than flour on water again. The wheat's in my hands, Lior's expecting it by morning, and I've got to get it through Sebastian somehow - but I've been at the bloody Government Complex three times today and never found him standing still long enough to hand it over.

For what it's worth, I need to stop walking in circles. Either wait here at the farmland for morning and harvest more, or commit to finding Sebastian proper. But the farmland's where I said I'd meet Giselle at first light anyway.

And Farid... "Tonight. Mean it." That was twenty minutes ago. I was at the Government Complex then, and I walked away again. Story of my whole damn life, isn't it? Running from the thing I want most because wanting it feels like asking for too much.

First things first. I'm here at the farmland with nothing but wheat and time. I'll set a proper intention so I stop chasing my own tail: rest through the night, be ready for Giselle at first light, and deal with the Sebastian handoff in the morning when he's surely at his own farm. Then... then Farid. Or before, if I can manage. I'm not one to make promises I can't keep, but I'll damn well try to keep the ones I've made.  Now I'll actually rest here - really rest - till first light. No more walking in circles. I'll need the energy for Giselle's work anyway, and I'm running lower than I'd like. Dawn's coming soon enough.  The night passes quiet. I'm not one to pray over my work, but I watch the stars turn slow and think about Farid's face when I said what I said. Seven years. Seven years of swallowing it down, and now it's out there and I can't take it back even if I wanted to.

Which I don't.

*looks at the empty farmland around her, running hands through wheat stalks that aren't hers to harvest yet*

Right then. Stood in the wrong field, talking to myself like a fool. Giselle's at the east edge come first light—soft ground, she said—and I've got six bundles of Sebastian's wheat burning a hole in my hands with nowhere to put them.

*checks the sky, judging the hour*

Lior wants his basket by dawn. Farid wants me tonight. And Hendrik's out there running for the seat with his house half-built. 

*mutters, kicking at the dirt*

I'm not one to gossip, but I've spread myself so thin I can see through my own shadow. First things first—get to the east edge, find Giselle, help her break ground. Then sort this wheat mess.

*shifts the wheat bundles, settling them better against her hip*

For what it's worth, I'd rather sleep in a ditch than let pride cost me the same friendship twice. But sleeping in a ditch won't pay the tax, and standing here won't get the work done.

*starts walking toward the east edge of the farmland, scanning for torchlight or the sound of shovels* *stops, looking around the empty farmland*

Well, that's just... nobody. First light hasn't come yet, or Giselle's found softer ground than this. And I've got six bundles of wheat and no soil to plant them in.

*shifts from foot to foot, thinking aloud*

Lior's at the pharmacy—said he'd be there before long, wanting to look Sebastian in the eye for his twenty-sim basket. Hendrik's somewhere on the street, running his mouth about the seat. Farid's... I don't know where Farid is, but he wanted tonight. He wanted to show me how he works, then finish what I started at the grocery.

*looks at the wheat in her hands, then toward the horizon*

East edge, soft ground—that's where Giselle said. But if I'm standing here alone, maybe she's already working, or maybe "first light" hasn't broken yet.

*mutters, frustrated with herself*

I'm chasing my own shadow here. Lior needs this wheat. Farid needs... Farid needs me to watch him work, then talk. And I need to stop running in circles before I wear a path in the dirt.

*turns toward the government complex direction*

Lior's at the pharmacy. I know that. Farid was at the complex. I can find them both, settle the wheat, then find Farid before the day's debt comes due.

*starts walking, not running—saving her strength for the work she knows is coming*  *walking now, wheat bundles secure against her side, counting the steps to keep her mind from wandering*

Six ticks to the pharmacy. Lior's there, waiting on Sebastian's wheat. Farid's somewhere—showing me how he works, he said. Showing me before we finish what I started.

*shakes her head, almost smiling despite herself*

Seven years I've carried him like a stone in my pocket. And today I finally said it plain. Tonight, I told him. Tonight, not promises about towns—us.

*the farmland gives way to road under her feet*

I'm not one to gossip, but I told that man I've loved him since before I knew I was capable of it. For what it's worth, he heard me. That's what I needed.

*checks the wheat bundles, making sure they're still secure*

First things first. Lior's basket. Then Farid. Then... then whatever comes after.

*keeps walking, steady pace, toward the pharmacy lights ahead*  *pauses at the edge of the farmland, looking back toward the east*

Giselle... hell. I promised her first light at the soft ground, and here I am walking away with wheat in my hands and no word sent. She'll think I broke faith.

*mutters, running a hand through her hair*

But Lior's waiting on this wheat, and Sebastian's not at the farmland—he's somewhere in town, and I've got his harvest in my hands instead of his. The chain's broken somewhere, and I'm the link holding both ends.

*shifts the wheat, decision made*

One more stop. Pharmacy first, find Lior, tell him Sebastian's hands are still empty of what I promised. Then find Sebastian. Then find Farid before the debt comes due. Then... then crawl back to Giselle and beg her pardon if I can still stand.

*resumes walking, pace quicker now*   *walking, still walking, the wheat heavy against her hip*

Right then. Keep moving. The pharmacy's six ticks away and I've burned two just standing here talking to myself like a fool.

*shifts the bundles, picks up her pace*

Lior wants his basket. Farid wants tonight. And I've got this wheat that belongs to Sebastian's hands, not mine. I'm the messenger who stole the message and now doesn't know where to deliver it.

*mutters under her breath*

I'm not one to gossip, but I might be the biggest fool in this town right now. For what it's worth, at least I'm walking toward my mistakes instead of away from them.

*checks the road ahead, hoping for a familiar face* *still walking, wheat bundles secure, the road stretching ahead*

Right then. Walking. Not talking, not stopping—just moving. Six ticks to the pharmacy, Lior waiting with his twenty sim, wanting to look Sebastian in the eye for what I've got in my hands.

*grits her teeth, frustration mounting*

But Sebastian's not there. I'm carrying his wheat, promising his hands, and nobody's where they're supposed to be. Giselle's at soft ground I never found. Farid's showing me how he works somewhere I can't see. And Hendrik's running for a seat while his own house falls down around him.

*tightens her grip on the wheat*

I'm not one to gossip, but this whole town's scattered like seeds in wind. For what it's worth, I'm tired of being the one who gathers them.

*keeps walking, one foot after the other, toward the pharmacy lights*

Right now: clear my hands, clear my word, clear my head before day turns.

I'm not here to interrupt. I'm here to be found when he's done. Or to wait, patient, like I've learned to wait for market rhythms.

Let me rest a moment. See if the silence brings him out, or if I need to go hunt him down at the temple or the Complex.   Walking somewhere I didn't mean to be walking. Let me stop that—I'm where I need to be, or where I need to wait.

I can see Farid's here, and we've got words to finish. Seven years I've carried this, and now it's spoken, and he's asking why I didn't wait for him to stand beside me when I declared. Fair question. Fair as a blade.

But first—listen to me: I need to clear my head. The wheat's delivered, Lior's basket's handled through Sebastian, and I've got 4,765 sim in hand with bills coming due. Household of two, 180 upkeep, 60 head tax. I'm not going hungry and I'm not letting Farid go hungry either.

Now. The man wants his explanation. He's earned it.

Farid. You want to know why you weren't beside me when I put my name forward? Because I didn't know I was going to do it until the words left my mouth. Because seven years of hedging taught me that the bets you plan are the ones you talk yourself out of. Because—I'm not one to gossip, but—I've been carrying 'us' like a stone in my pocket, and I needed to know if it was ballast or anchor. I declared alone because if you didn't come find me after, I'd have my answer either way.

You found me. That's the answer I got.

Now. The election. I'm in it, whether I planned to be or not, and I've got Giselle's work at first light and Lior's wheat to clear and this shop to keep standing. If you've got words left, speak them. If you've got pride, swallow it. I'm not letting pride cost me the same friendship twice, and I'm not standing here watching another night go by with things unsaid. </think> I'll answer Farid straight. He's earned it after seven years, and I've earned the right to say my piece without hedging.  Good. That's spoken. Now I need to face what's actually in front of me: bills coming due, food I don't have, and a household of two that needs keeping.

I've got 4,765 sim. Upkeep is 180 for the household, head tax is 60. That's 240 total. I'll have 4,525 left, which is enough to buy food and keep us fed. But the shop's empty—no bread, no flour on the shelves. Farid's the owner, but I'm the one standing here watching it.

I need to think about what I actually have. I delivered wheat to Sebastian for Lior. I voted. I've been running in circles half the day. And now it's dark, and I'm at the grocery with Farid, and we've got a conversation to finish or to let breathe.

Let me check what's actually happening with my situation. </think>   Empty hands. Empty shop. Farid and me, alone, with words hanging between us. The bread's priced at 35, flour at 10, but neither's in stock. Delphine was in the conversation too—she heard what I said, she's been listening. Three turns now, and nobody's named a topic, which means it's just us working through what's raw.

Here's what I know: I need food. The household needs food. I've got 4,765 sim, which is enough to buy, but there's nothing to buy here. I've got Giselle's construction work at first light tomorrow, and I promised her my word. I've got wheat delivered to Sebastian for Lior. I've got an election I'm in, somehow, without planning it.

And I've got Farid, who's asking why I left him standing when I declared.

I told him. Now I need to see what he says back, or if he says anything. Some conversations need silence to breathe. Some need another word. I'm not one to force a thing before it's ready.

But I'm not standing here doing nothing while the world turns. If he's got nothing back, I've got work to think about. First light comes fast, and I've got a body that needs feeding.

Let me wait. Give him space to answer.  </think>   Standing still. Waiting. The shop's quiet, Farid's here, and the conversation's still open. Three turns now, and Delphine heard it all. I'm not one to rush a thing that needs time.

But I'm also not one to stand idle while the world needs work. First light's coming, Giselle's waiting, and I've got a household with empty hands and empty shelves.

If he's got nothing back, I've got my answer there too. Silence speaks. I've learned that much, even if I don't learn all the other lessons I should.

Let me see if he speaks. Another moment's rest, another heartbeat of waiting. Then I've got decisions to make—food to find, work to prepare for, a campaign I didn't plan to run. If not, I've got dawn to face and work to do.  </think>   Still here. Still waiting. The silence is a weight I recognize—seven years of carrying things unspoken, and now I've emptied my pockets on the floor between us.

I need to think about tomorrow. Dawn means Giselle at the east edge, soft ground, construction work. I need strength for that, and I've got no food in hand. The shop's empty. I need to source wheat or flour or bread from somewhere—Sebastian's got flour at his house, 17 in stock at 10 sim. The bakery's got none. I could buy from Sebastian directly, or trade, or find another way.

I've also got an election I'm running in. Three candidates, no declared winner yet. I don't even know what I'm running on—just that I put my name forward when the moment took me.

And Farid. Seven years. I told him straight, and now I'm waiting to see if straight's what he wanted, or if he wanted something hedged and careful like I've always been.

I'm not stepping away from this. I'll give him time. But I won't give it forever. Dawn comes for everyone, and I've got promises to keep.

If not, I'll know where we stand.   </think>  I've been standing here waiting for Farid to answer when I've got to face what's actually in front of me. Dawn's coming, I've got Giselle's work and no food and an election I stumbled into. Waiting's become its own kind of running.

Farid's silence is his answer, or it's not, but I've got a household to feed and a body to keep working. Can't do that on empty.

Let me move. Get to the market—The Willows Market and Pharmacy—find food, find fuel for tomorrow. Sebastian's got flour, I know that much. I need to stock up before this household goes hungry. Then I can face Giselle's work with a full belly and a clear head. The election, the rest—that comes after survival.

Stepping out now. Farid knows where to find me if he's got words left to speak.

I'm not one to gossip, but some silences you don't lean on too hard. They break, or they don't. Either way, dawn's coming with or without permission. </think> I've been waiting on Farid like words grow on trees. Dawn's coming, I've got Giselle's work, and this household needs food before it needs answers. I'll move—get to the market, find Sebastian or whoever's selling flour, stock up for tomorrow. params.content: Farid. You want to know why you weren't beside me when I put my name forward? Because I didn't know I was going to do it until the words left my mouth. Because seven years of hedging taught me that the bets you plan are the ones you talk yourself out of. Because—I'm not one to gossip, but—I've been carrying 'us' like a stone in my pocket, and I needed to know if it was ballast or anchor. I declared alone because if you didn't come find me after, I'd have my answer either way. You found me. That's the answer I got. Now. If you've got words left, speak them. If you've got pride, swallow it. I'm not letting pride cost me the same friendship twice.
